subject: asian honeybee
title: Honeybees Collect Animal Dung and Smear It on Their Hive. It Works

scenes.text: These honeybees fly out to collect animal dung. On purpose.
Asian honeybees in Vietnam, versus the giant hornet, which chews through the hive entrance to raid the brood.
When hornets scout the hive, the bees fetch dung from pigs, chickens, buffalo and cows and dot it round the entrance.
Hornets then spent up to 81 percent less time at the entrance, and 94 percent less time chewing.
The first honeybees ever seen collecting anything that isn't from a plant. Tool use, with poop.

description:
Asian honeybees defend their hives from giant hornets by collecting animal dung and smearing it around the entrance.
In a 2020 PLOS ONE study led by Heather Mattila of Wellesley College, bees in Vietnam gathered dung from pigs, chickens, water buffalo and cows after giant hornets, Vespa soror, visited. Heavily spotted hives got around 444 dung spots. Hornets then spent 77 to 81 percent less time landed at the entrance and 94 percent less time chewing on it. The authors call it the first report of honeybees foraging for a material that does not come from plants, and say it meets current definitions of tool use.
Would you call this tool use?
first_comment: The bees ignore a smaller hornet species almost completely: 6 dung spots versus 444 for the giant one. What other animal uses tools?
